doc.title: Rick Margitza interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 22, 2024

title: Composing away from the piano; influence versus plagiarism
summary: He tries starting from sax, groove or movies instead of piano, and they trade quotes on influence (Pepper Adams).

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Well not complet — I mean I kind of came up with this little descending line and then I tinkered with it. So when I improvised it it wasn’t in its final form but I just kind of came up with that melody as a result of hearing the ostinato in the chords. And I mean these days there’s a — I think it’s from Pat Metheny, he said, “Everybody has about seven or eight tunes in them and they keep writing different versions of that same tune.” So I’m getting to that point where I’m repeating myself, or I feel like I’m repeating myself so I’m forcing myself to compose in different ways so I’m trying to not start with the piano anymore. Since my piano playing is somewhat limited I tend to move in the same harmonic worlds or the same kind of things that feel good under my hands. So now I’m trying to maybe just find a melody on the saxophone first or maybe find a drum beat or some type of groove [phone rings] sorry.

Like I can totally relate to that. Because I usually start at the piano myself and like I’m not a fantastic piano player so I do find that I’m trying to put my hands down in different ways. Like, and you mentioned bass notes, like instead of thinking before your hands hit, okay I’m going to do some E flat thing, like just put your hands down and see what happens.

Yes exactly. Just forcing myself just to come from different places and that’s actually kind of been fruitful. I found a couple of — not full songs yet — but things that feel different. And it might also be something — I’ll be watching a movie or a TV show and just hear a groove that wouldn’t be something that I would normally start with and you just kind of do a little bit of — I don’t know whose quote this is but they say, “In literature it’s plagiarism but in music it’s influence.”

I think I can remember this — Pepper Adams — Jerry Dodgion told me this story of Pepper Adams, they were in front of a whole group of students and you know they were talking about influences and so forth, and Pepper said, “If you take from one person it’s plagiarism, if you take from everybody it’s research.”
That’s a good one. That’s really good.
